properties.title: LP NS Global Hydrogen Abundance - Calibrated ppm (Lawrence et al., 2022)
properties.lri:data_use_note: Quantitative global H abundance in ppm, calibrated to Apollo sample hydrogen measurements. This is the most accurately calibrated global H map available from LP-NS data. Use for resource estimation, spatial prospecting, and regional comparison. Wilson et al. 2018 is the upstream spatial input to this map — both have the same effective resolution (~50-61 km). Average global H: 47 ± ~10 ppm (systematic uncertainty from Apollo calibration).
properties.apollo_calibration_note: H abundance calibrated using Apollo soil and regolith breccia hydrogen abundances compiled by Haskin & Warren (1991). These materials best represent the bulk soils sampled by orbital neutron data. Calibration links REE-corrected epithermal count rates to absolute ppm values.
properties.polar_h_enhancement_note: Bulk hydrogen abundances only increase clearly poleward of 75°-80° latitude (Lawrence et al. 2022, Section 4 / Figure 8). Equatorward of this threshold, H is relatively flat at 30-50 ppm driven by solar wind implantation, with no significant latitude dependence.
properties.h_kreep_note: KREEP-rich regions (Th > 8 ppm) show absolute H of 61-83 ppm, with 14-36 ppm excess above the 47 ppm solar-wind baseline. Enhancement persists across soil maturities, indicating endogenous origin not solar-wind accumulation (Section 6.2). High-KREEP prospecting targets should expect H in this range.
properties.h_omat_note: Immature surfaces (fresh impact ejecta, high OMAT) show ~20 ppm lower H than the global mean due to insufficient solar-wind implantation time (Section 5.3). When prospecting near young craters, expect H significantly below the 47 ppm baseline. Cross-reference with optical maturity maps before targeting.

h_reservoirs.aristarchus_water_mass_note: Estimated from 50-68 ppm H, ~20 m deposit thickness, 49013 km² area, 1.5 g/cm³ soil density (Section 6.1). Comparable in order of magnitude to polar PSR estimates (2×10⁸ - 2.5×10¹⁰ t). Paper identifies Aristarchus as an attractive ISRU landing site target.
h_reservoirs.note: Other deposits (Humorum, Rima Bode, Sulpicius Gallus) too small to detect with LP 50 km footprint
Dominant H source for non-polar non-pyroclastic regions; correlated with surface maturity (OMAT)
Latitude-dependent, near-zero equatorward of 30°; rises to ~56-80 ppm H equivalent poleward; stable above ~60° latitude
Up to few wt% WEH; LP 50 km footprint cannot resolve individual PSRs — bulk values include footprint averaging with surrounding terrain

properties.measurement_depth: few tens of centimeters (bulk subsurface, not surface)
properties.authors: D. J. Lawrence, P. N. Peplowski, J. T. Wilson, R. C. Elphic
properties.lri:quality_note: Global hydrogen abundance map in ppm from Lawrence et al. (2022, Figure 6). This is the primary scientific result of the paper and the most accurately calibrated global H product from LP-NS data. The processing chain is: (1) raw LP-NS epithermal count rates (Maurice et al. 2004) → (2) Wilson et al. 2018 pixon reconstruction (noise suppression, same ~50-61 km effective resolution) → (3) REE-corrected count rates (removes neutron absorption bias from Sm/Gd in KREEP terranes) → (4) calibrated H ppm using Apollo sample measurements (this map). Global average H is 47 ± ~10 ppm, max 117 ppm — values ~25% lower than Lawrence et al. (2006) and significantly lower than Lawrence et al. (2015) which had polar values up to 180 ppm; difference attributed to the improved REE correction and Apollo calibration. Consistent with solar wind implantation as the dominant H source for non-polar, non-pyroclastic regions. Key features: Aristarchus Plateau shows confirmed bulk H enhancement (50-68 ppm) extending to tens of cm depth (not merely surficial); KREEP-rich regions show absolute H of 61-83 ppm (14-36 ppm excess above solar-wind baseline); immature surfaces (young craters, fresh ejecta) show ~20 ppm deficit below global mean; polar enhancements present but LP 50 km footprint cannot resolve individual PSRs. Five distinct H reservoirs identified: pyroclastic deposits, KREEP-rich materials, bulk solar-wind, surface OH/H2O, and PSRs (see h_reservoirs field). ISRU relevance: unlike count-rate maps, these ppm values can be directly used in resource estimation calculations. However, at 47 ppm bulk average, global regolith H is a marginal ISRU feedstock — polar PSR enhancements (not fully resolved here) represent the primary water-ice ISRU target. This map is most useful for: (1) establishing baseline H inventory for non-polar sites; (2) identifying regionally elevated H (pyroclastic deposits, polar regions) for prospecting prioritization; (3) cross-correlating H with Th/REE/OMAT to disentangle source mechanisms.
properties.processing:lineage: Upstream NS data reduction: Maurice et al. (2004). Pixon spatial reconstruction: Wilson et al. (2018) — adopted as the base epithermal map for all Lawrence et al. (2022) analyses (Section 2). REE correction applied to reconstructed count rates using macroscopic absorption cross-section map (Peplowski et al. 2016) to remove Sm/Gd absorption bias. H ppm calibration applied using Apollo soil and regolith breccia hydrogen abundances (Haskin & Warren 1991) following Lawrence et al. (2022, Sections 3-4). Source file: figure6.txt from JHU-APL data repository (https://lib.jhuapl.edu//papers/global-hydrogen-abundances-on-the-moon/). COG production: comment lines stripped; (MAPLON, MAPLAT, HMAP) triplets sorted north→south, west→east; reshaped to 360×720; written as AAIGrid; gdal_translate to COG with IAU:30100 CRS, DEFLATE/PREDICTOR=3 compression.
